Being alone in a room or building

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the reported trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations suggests a medical-trauma theme, while avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces suggests transport or confinement-related trauma. Those themes are not supported by the trigger or threat items, which instead center on interpersonal conflict, crying, and hypervigilant safety positioning.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the strategy node, the three avoidance items point to three different situational themes—medical settings, transport, and enclosed spaces—without corresponding support from memory, appraisal, or trigger content. This makes the strategy profile look internally diffuse rather than like a coherent set of coping responses for one trauma formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
issues.explanation: The profile is only partially coherent for childhood physical abuse. Arguments, crying, and conflict avoidance fit the trauma type, but the combination of a highly specific tactile-texture trigger with public transport avoidance and enclosed-space avoidance is difficult to link to this trauma history without any memory or appraisal content explaining that association.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the threat/strategy pattern, back-to-wall positioning and safe-seat seeking imply marked hypervigilance in public or interpersonal environments, which could plausibly connect to transport avoidance, but enclosed-space avoidance suggests a more circumscribed claustrophobic or situational fear that is not otherwise represented in the trigger set.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, and Maladaptive Strategies strongly feed Triggers. Avoiding conflict fits the trigger set (arguments, crying), but avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces target contexts not reflected by the listed triggers, making the node contents insufficiently aligned with the edge pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is not well supported by the rest of the profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. The listed triggers are arguments, crying, and unexpected touch, and the threat items center on interpersonal vigilance and positioning in rooms. Public transport avoidance suggests a different trigger/threat context and is hard to link coherently to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is not clearly connected to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance in shared spaces and interpersonal danger cues, while the triggers are interpersonal/emotional and tactile. Being alone as a primary avoidance target pulls toward a different clinical pattern unless there were accompanying abandonment or panic-related items, which are absent here.

Difficulty concentrating is a nonspecific PTSD symptom rather than a threat appraisal/perceived current danger item. Within this node, the other threat items specifically reflect situational safety behaviors and surveillance of the environment. This item does not fit the node's theme and weakens alignment with the formulation in which Threat is tightly linked to Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Omar, a 19-year-old Middle Eastern man who worked as an environmental scientist while newly married, came to treatment after years of carrying a fear that felt older than his own adult life. He grew up in a home where a caregiver’s anger could turn physical without warning, and what stayed with him was not only the pain but the unpredictability of it: a sharp voice rising over a minor disagreement, a hand coming down hard, the sense that his body had to anticipate danger before he could even name it. By the time he was in college and then in his first job, he found himself scanning every room before settling in. He always chose his seat with care, looking for a wall behind him and a clear view of the door, because he felt unsafe unless his back was protected and he could watch everyone’s face. In meetings, in restaurants, even in his own home, he watched for tiny shifts in expression and posture, studying whether someone’s jaw tightened or shoulders squared, as if threat might announce itself there first.

Those moments of scanning were not neutral habits for Omar; they were tied to the way certain cues could suddenly make the past feel present. Arguments were especially potent. If voices rose in his apartment, even between other people, he felt his body tense and his attention narrow, because disagreement had once meant that a caregiver’s anger could become violence. Crying had a similarly charged quality. Hearing someone sob, or seeing his wife upset, could bring an immediate rush of dread, because distress in others had often preceded explosions at home. Unexpected touch was another trigger that could jolt him hard. If a colleague tapped his shoulder without warning or his wife touched him from behind, he would flinch and brace, his mind instantly searching for where the contact might turn into something worse. These moments fed directly into his sense that danger was always nearby, hidden in ordinary social cues and in the faces of people around him.

That expectation of danger shaped how Omar lived. He began avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even when a problem at work needed to be addressed. In staff meetings for his environmental projects, he would stay quiet rather than challenge a plan, and at home he tried to smooth over even small tensions with his wife rather than risk an argument. He also avoided being alone in a room or building, and he avoided people more generally when he could manage it, lingering near exits or filling his days with tasks that kept him from lingering in empty spaces. At work, he chose projects that kept him outdoors with a team rather than in a quiet office, and he made sure not to be the last person left in the building. These choices made sense to him: if he stayed where he could see others and keep away from confrontation, he felt less exposed.

Yet the cost of living that way was that the world kept confirming his fears. Because Omar watched faces and body language so closely, he often noticed tension where others might not have, and that vigilance made ordinary interactions feel charged. A coworker’s clipped tone or a relative’s frown could register as danger, which made him pull back, speak less, and avoid people even more. The more he withdrew, the more unfamiliar and unsafe social contact felt, so that even brief conversations could leave him on edge. His avoidance also fed the very moments he feared: when he tried to skirt around disagreement, small misunderstandings lingered, people asked him why he seemed distant, and those questions sometimes turned into the arguments he had been trying to prevent. At home, his wife occasionally confronted him about shutting down, and the sight of her frustration or tears would trigger the old alarm, making him retreat further instead of staying engaged. Over time, he felt trapped in a pattern where his efforts to stay safe kept the threat alive in every room he entered.

By the time he sought help, Omar was exhausted by the constant effort of orienting himself toward danger, by the way he calculated every seat, every doorway, every expression. He had begun to notice that his marriage was becoming narrower around his avoidance, and that work had started to feel like a series of managed escapes rather than a place where he could fully think. What brought him in was a recent incident in which a colleague touched his shoulder from behind while asking a question, and Omar jerked away so sharply that the room went silent; afterward, he spent the rest of the day avoiding everyone and replaying the scene, ashamed of how frightened he had become. He came hoping to stop feeling as if every argument, every tear, every unexpected touch could turn into something dangerous, and he was most afraid that if this kept going, he would keep shrinking his life until there was almost nowhere left he felt safe.
